planting.note: Site where the trunk gets winter sun so the exfoliating bark colors up; avoid hot, humid summer climates that stress birch roots.

directions: Native to central China, this wild birch species peels in curling sheets of orange-pink to coppery bark that brightens with age, giving it a bark display rivaling the more commonly grown cultivated birches. Plant in cool-summer climates with consistently moist, well-drained soil, since like most birches it resents prolonged heat and drought stress. Keep the root zone mulched and cool, and avoid compacted or poorly drained sites that invite bronze birch borer. Fall leaf color is a modest yellow, so the trunk is the main seasonal interest.

planting.note: Tolerates a wider range of summer heat than paper birch, making it a sturdier bark-interest tree for marginal birch climates.

directions: This wild birch from Japan, Korea, and the Russian Far East sheds creamy white to pinkish-tan bark in papery curls, with older trunks taking on a rougher, chalkier texture than paper birch. It performs reliably in cold-winter regions and shows better resistance to summer stress and bronze birch borer than many North American birches when given adequate soil moisture. Grow in full sun with consistently moist, well-drained soil, and avoid heavy clay that stays waterlogged. Yellow fall foliage follows a season of steady, pest-tolerant growth.

planting.note: Needs plenty of room to reach its mature size; site away from structures and underground utilities.

directions: Native to Japan, this is the largest-leaved of all birches, with heart-shaped leaves to 6 inches long and orange-brown to gray bark that peels in thin horizontal strips. It grows into a substantial shade tree given room, and prefers cool, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Because it resents heat and drought, it performs best in northern or high-elevation gardens rather than hot lowland climates. Fall color is a clean yellow that shows well against the pale trunk.

planting.note: Grows as a slow, multi-stemmed shrub rather than a single-trunk tree; useful where a smaller-scale birch is wanted.

directions: Unlike its tree-form relatives, this shrubby wild birch from the Caucasus and northeastern Turkey has non-peeling gray-brown bark and unusually large, bold leaves for a birch, turning rich gold in autumn. It stays compact and slow-growing, making it suitable for smaller gardens where a towering white-bark birch would overwhelm the space. Grow in full sun in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil, and avoid hot, dry sites. Its multi-stemmed habit and oversized foliage give it a distinct texture among birches.

planting.note: Site to show off the winter bark; underplant with low groundcover rather than turf to avoid trunk damage from mowers.

directions: This Chinese wild species is one of the classic snakebark maples, with smooth green bark striped vertically in white and leaves that are simple and unlobed, unusual among maples and easy to mistake for an entirely different genus. It grows as a graceful small tree, tolerating part shade better than most maples and benefiting from protection from harsh afternoon sun in warmer zones. Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil and keep roots cool with mulch. Fall color runs from yellow to soft orange, but the striped winter bark is the main event.

planting.note: Give afternoon shade in warmer parts of its range to prevent leaf scorch on the thin foliage.

directions: Native to Japan, this snakebark maple has young stems tinged red over white vertical striations, with red petioles carrying three-lobed leaves that turn shades of red and orange in fall. It is a woodland-edge species that prefers the dappled light and even moisture of a shaded understory rather than open, exposed sites. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil and shelter from strong wind, which can scorch the relatively thin leaves. The combination of colored bark and fall foliage gives it two distinct seasons of interest.

planting.note: Best used as a shaded understory accent where its unusual non-maple-like foliage can be appreciated up close.

directions: Among wild maples this Japanese species is a curiosity: its simple, unlobed, finely serrated leaves look almost exactly like a hornbeam's rather than a typical maple's, which is how it earned its common name. It stays small and tolerates considerably more shade than most maples, making it a good choice for a woodland understory where typical lobed-leaf maples would struggle. Grow in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil protected from hot afternoon sun. Fall color is a quiet yellow, secondary to its novelty foliage.

planting.note: Dioecious species; fruiting occurs only where both male and female trees are present.

directions: This Japanese wild maple bears trifoliate leaves made up of three separate leaflets, giving the whole tree a look closer to Boston ivy or poison ivy than a classic maple. It is dioecious, with separate male and female trees, and its clean yellow fall color and fine texture suit it to a woodland-edge planting with afternoon shade. Grow in moist, well-drained soil and shelter from strong, drying wind. It stays smaller and more graceful than most shade-tree maples, fitting easily into a mixed border planting.

planting.note: One of the more drought-tolerant maples once established; avoid overwatering, especially on heavier soils.

directions: Native across the Mediterranean basin, this small, slow-growing wild maple has thick, leathery, three-lobed leaves that persist semi-evergreen in mild winters and resist the leaf scorch that troubles many maples in hot, dry conditions. It tolerates poor, rocky, alkaline soil and drought far better than most maples, making it a practical choice for Mediterranean-climate or xeriscape plantings rather than a moist woodland setting. Plant in full sun with sharp drainage, and avoid rich, consistently wet soil. Fall color is a subdued yellow, secondary to its toughness and fine-textured form.
